reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: Results from infarction of the dorsolateral medulla, most often due to intracranial vertebral artery disease rather than a discrete posterior inferior cerebellar artery occlusion
The hallmark is a crossed sensory pattern: ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature over the face with contralateral loss over the trunk and limbs
Vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus reflect vestibular nucleus involvement and are frequently the presenting complaint
Ipsilateral Horner syndrome (partial ptosis, miosis, facial anhidrosis) arises from disruption of the descending sympathetic fibres
Dysphagia, hoarseness, and reduced gag reflex follow nucleus ambiguus involvement and carry a genuine aspiration risk
Ipsilateral limb and gait ataxia occur from inferior cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar involvement, and intractable hiccups may be prominent
Motor power is characteristically preserved because the pyramidal tract lies ventromedially and is spared
reference.pathophysiology: The syndrome follows ischaemia of the dorsolateral medulla oblongata, a territory supplied by penetrating branches of the intracranial vertebral artery and the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Because vertebral disease is the usual culprit, the infarct straddles several closely packed structures: the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract (ipsilateral facial sensory loss), the crossed spinothalamic tract (contralateral body sensory loss), the vestibular nuclei (vertigo and nystagmus), the nucleus ambiguus (dysphagia and hoarseness), the descending sympathetic pathway (Horner syndrome), and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (ipsilateral ataxia). The medial position of the corticospinal tract explains the preservation of limb strength, producing the classic dissociated, crossed clinical picture.
additionalDifferentials: Vestibular neuronitis or acute peripheral vertigo
Demyelinating plaque of the brainstem in multiple sclerosis
Vertebral artery dissection presenting with posterior circulation ischaemia
additionalInvestigations: Diffusion-weighted MRI of the brainstem to confirm acute dorsolateral medullary infarction
MR or CT angiography of the vertebrobasilar system to identify vertebral stenosis or dissection
HINTS bedside oculomotor examination to distinguish central from peripheral vertigo
Formal swallow assessment to quantify aspiration risk before oral intake
Cardiac and vascular risk workup including ECG and lipid and glucose profiling
Vessel wall imaging where dissection or intracranial atherosclerosis is suspected
redFlags: Progressive drowsiness or new long-tract signs suggesting brainstem or cerebellar swelling with mass effect
Silent aspiration with subsequent pneumonia in an apparently mild presentation
Vertebral artery dissection with risk of recurrent embolism or basilar extension
Central vertigo mistaken for benign peripheral disease and discharged
reference.prognosis: Many patients recover functional swallowing and gait over weeks to months, though disabling ataxia, persistent dysphagia, or central neuropathic facial pain can remain; overall outcome is generally more favourable than for medial or ventral brainstem strokes.
pitfalls: Attributing isolated vertigo and vomiting to a peripheral labyrinthine cause and missing the stroke
Allowing oral feeding before a formal swallow assessment and precipitating aspiration
Overlooking a subtle ipsilateral Horner syndrome that would localise the lesion
Assuming preserved limb power excludes a significant brainstem infarct
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
management: Manage as an acute posterior-circulation stroke, considering intravenous thrombolysis within the window then antiplatelet therapy, while imaging for vertebral artery dissection which may instead warrant anticoagulation
Institute secondary prevention with antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy, high-intensity statin, and control of blood pressure, glucose, and other vascular risk factors
Keep nil by mouth until formal swallow assessment, using nasogastric feeding and aspiration precautions given the high dysphagia and aspiration risk
Treat vertigo and nausea with vestibular sedatives and antiemetics, and control intractable hiccups with agents such as baclofen or chlorpromazine
Manage persistent central neuropathic facial pain with neuropathic agents
Provide multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy for ataxia and speech-and-language therapy for swallowing and voice
Monitor for cerebellar swelling and brainstem compression, escalating to neurosurgical care if deterioration occurs
